section: Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of Newborn (PPHN) › Oxygenation index, Diagnosis modality, Oxygen therapy (intentional use of increased FiO2), Airway management, Hemodynamic support

scope.population: Term and near-term (late preterm) newborn infants, about ≥34 weeks' gestation, with suspected or confirmed PPHN, without congenital diaphragmatic hernia unless stated. The manual limits its airway and iNO lines to ≥35 weeks; line 46 separately names infants <35 weeks, so evidence on preterm infants counts for that line only.
scope.topic: Grading, recognition and acute management of PPHN: oxygenation index, diagnosis, intentional oxygen therapy, airway and arterial access, and hemodynamic support with vasoactive drugs.
scope.basis: Cardiovascular chapter, heading 'Persistent Pulmonary Hypertension of Newborn (PPHN)' (line 6) and subheadings at lines 8, 19, 25, 42 and 48, read with '## Population context' of evidence_sheet.md.

claims.manual_text: $Oxygenation\ index\ (OI)\ =\ \frac{FiO_{2}\times{MAP}}{PaO_{2}}$
claims.summary: Published definitions carry a ×100 term when FiO2 is a fraction, or enter FiO2 as a percentage [ELSO2013; Rawat2015; Ball2023; Mohamed2026; Hilgendorff2016], and the PaO2 site varies, post-ductal in ELSO and typically pre-ductal in one review [ELSO2013; Chandrasekharan2020].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests the index is calculated with a ×100 term when FiO2 is a fraction, or with FiO2 entered as a percentage, the scale on which published severity and ECMO values are set [ELSO2013; Rawat2015; Ball2023; Hilgendorff2016]. The sampling site also affects the value: ELSO specifies post-ductal PaO2, and a UK review advises recording the site [ELSO2013; Mohamed2026].

evidence.quote: Oxygenation Index: Mean airway P x FiO2 x 100
Post ductal PaO2
evidence.location: I.A Indications, p3 (denominator of the OI formula)

evidence.quote: Oxygenation index (OI=mean airway pressure MAP × FiO2 × 100÷PaO2) is used to assess severity of hypoxic respiratory failure (HRF) and persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn (PPHN).
For this calculation, the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) is entered as a percentage
(OI): FiO 2%×MAP/pO2
evidence.location: Oxygenation index definition in the iNO paragraph

evidence.quote: FiO₂ should be expressed as a fraction.
The sampling site must therefore be stated whenever the index is recorded or handed over
Preductal arterial oxygenation (PaO2) is typically used to assess the severity (based on oxygenation index), management, and evaluate response to therapy in PPHN
evidence.location: Section 2.9, Arterial Oxygen Tension and Its Effect on PPHN

claims.manual_text: Severity: - 5-15: Mild - 15-25: Moderate - 25-40: Severe
claims.summary: A pooled analysis of three iNO trials in infants ≥34 weeks stratified OI as ≤15 mild, >15 to ≤25 moderate, >25 to ≤40 severe and >40 very severe [Golombek2010], a 2025 review instead grades <10, 10-25 and >25 [Chojnacka2025], and no guideline grading of OI bands was among the retrieved sources.

evidence.quote: stratified based on the OI (< or = 15 = mild, >15 to < or = 25 = moderate, >25 to < or = 40 = severe, >40 = very severe)
OI < 10: This range suggests mild hypoxemia.
OI 10–25: Values within this range represent moderate hypoxemia.
OI > 25: An OI greater than 25 indicates severe hypoxemia and implies a significant risk of pulmonary dysfunction.

claims.manual_text: Severity: - >40: Consider ECMO if all interventions exhausted
claims.summary: ELSO v1.3 (2013) and a one-centre guideline give OI >40 for >4 hours or OI >20 without improvement after about 24 hours [ELSO2013; Ball2023], CHOP treats OI >25 over 4-6 hours as a referral trajectory, separate from cannulation [CHOP2026], and the current 2020 ELSO guideline lists an OI with sustained elevation and no improvement among its indications without a numerical threshold [Wild2020; Mohamed2026]; AHA/ATS guidance, as reported in a review, gives OI >40 as an indication to consider referral [Mohamed2026], and another review calls OI >40 a generally accepted criterion to start ECMO [Lakshminrusimha2015].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests OI >40 remains a recognized ECMO trigger, as an indication to consider referral in AHA/ATS guidance reported in a review and as a generally accepted criterion in another review [Mohamed2026; Lakshminrusimha2015], with ELSO v1.3 and one guideline adding a duration of >4 hours and a second route of OI >20 without improvement after about 24 hours [ELSO2013; Ball2023]. Referral to an ECMO-capable centre is treated as a separate, earlier step, at OI >25 and while stabilization options remain [CHOP2026; Chojnacka2025]. The 2020 ELSO guideline gives no OI number [Wild2020].

evidence.quote: Neonates with severe respiratory failure,  refractory to maximal medical management, with a potentially reversible etiology.
1.  Oxygenation Index > 40 for >4 hours
2. Oxygenation Index >20 with lack of improvement despite prolonged (>24h) maximal medical therapy or persistent episodes of decompensation
Typically, an OI threshold of 40 for at least 4 hours, or over 20 for 24 hours despite medical optimization, is utilized for ECMO therapy.
Oxygenation Index exceeding 25 over 4-6 hours despite implemented changes.
evidence.location: Referral to an ECMO-Capable Center (Conditional Recommendation: trajectories that may prompt ECMO referral)

evidence.quote: Referral to an ECMO-capable center should occur while additional stabilization options remain available and before the development of refractory hypoxemia or circulatory collapse.
evidence.location: Referral to an ECMO-Capable Center (Strong Recommendation)

evidence.quote: The traditional ECMO OI starting threshold was 40 for more than 4 h; however, it is reasonable to consider contacting the ECMO center when, despite implemented therapies, OI still remains above 25, in order to prepare earlier for transportation logistics [28].
3. Oxygenation Index with sustained elevation and no improvement
evidence.location: Figure 1, Indications, contraindications, and modes of support (transcribed from the figure image)

evidence.quote: The current 2020 guideline describes the criterion as sustained elevation of the OI without improvement, without specifying a numerical threshold
evidence.location: Review: oxygenation index (ELSO documents, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: An OI above 40 is an indication to consider referral to an ECMO center [13].
evidence.location: Review: Quantifying Severity: The Oxygenation Index in Kilopascals (AHA/ATS guideline, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: Across the documents examined, however, thresholds above 25, 30, and 40 are used, and no single figure represents a universal ECMO criterion.
evidence.location: Review: Quantifying Severity: The Oxygenation Index in Kilopascals

evidence.quote: Generally accepted criteria to start ECMO are persistent hypoxemia (with an OI of >40 or alveolar-arterial gradient >600 despite aggressive medical management of PPHN with mechanical ventilation and iNO) and the presence of hemodynamic instability (Fig 6).
evidence.location: ECMO paragraph, after heading "Chronic Pulmonary Hypertension in Neonates"

claims.manual_text: - Clinical suspicion: high oxygen needs, labile $SpO_{2}$ (huge swing)
claims.summary: Labile hypoxemia is described as characteristic of PPHN and the basis of clinical diagnosis [Lakshminrusimha2015; Singh2021; Ball2023], and difficulty maintaining oxygenation despite escalating support is called the most important clinical feature [Mohamed2026].

evidence.quote: Labile hypoxemia (marked change in oxygen saturation with minimal or no change in ventilator settings or fraction of inspired oxygen [FIO2]) is characteristic of PPHN
The diagnosis of PPHN is based on clinical evidence of labile hypoxemia often associated with differential cyanosis and confirmed by echocardiography.
Hypoxemia is often labile in PPHN, unlike fixed hypoxemia seen in cyanotic CHD (4–6).
Newborns with PPHN are typically labile, secondary to their “reactive” pulmonary vascular bed.
However, the most important clinical feature is difficulty maintaining adequate oxygenation despite escalating respiratory support [3].
evidence.location: Review: Recognizing PPHN in a level 2 unit

claims.manual_text: - Pre- and post-ductal $SpO_{2}$ differential > 10%
claims.summary: CHOP, a one-centre guideline and a review use a gap of 5-10% or >5-10% [CHOP2026; Ball2023; Singh2021], while the EPPVDN algorithm and one UK network use >10% [Hilgendorff2016; Mohamed2026]; the gap can be absent with a closed duct or atrial shunting, so its absence does not exclude PPHN [Lakshminrusimha2015; Mohamed2026].

evidence.quote: Clinical guidance: A pre- to post-ductal SpO₂ gradient >5–10% supports right-to-left shunting consistent with PPHN physiology.
A pre-ductal saturation measuring 5 to 10% over the post-ductal saturation is highly suggestive of PPHN.

Saturation differences of greater than 5%–10% or PaO2 differences of 10–20 mm Hg between right upper limb and lower limbs, with pre-ductal levels being higher than post-ductal levels, are considered significant.
PH needs to be considered when tricuspid regurgitation (TR) jet >2.5m/sec (Echo) and preductal/postductal oxygen saturation differences >10%.
Pre- to post-ductal gap above 10% marks significant right-to-left shunting.
evidence.location: Table 2, section B (regional network, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: The UK guidelines examined are clear that the absence of a saturation gap does not exclude PPHN [1,3].
If the PDA is closed and the shunt exclusively is at the PFO level, the degree of cyanosis is similar in both the upper and lower limbs.

claims.manual_text: - Echocardiography STAT
claims.summary: Echocardiography is the diagnostic gold standard [Singh2021; Lakshminrusimha2015] and CHOP asks for it urgently, with a goal of before or within 6-12 hours of diagnosis or iNO initiation [CHOP2026].

evidence.quote: Echocardiography is the diagnostic gold standard for PPHN and should be obtained urgently (goal: prior to or within 6-12 hours of diagnosis or iNO initiation)
Echocardiography is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis of PPHN, monitor the response to the therapeutic interventions and rule out underlying cyanotic or critical CHD.
Echocardiography is the gold standard to confirm the diagnosis and to monitor the efficacy of specific therapeutic interventions in PPHN (Fig 3).

claims.manual_text: - Oxygen is the first-line therapy for PPHN.
claims.summary: Oxygen is described as a potent pulmonary vasodilator and adequate oxygenation as the mainstay or cornerstone of care, and the EPPVDN gives oxygen to a pre-ductal target a Class I recommendation [Singh2021; Chandrasekharan2020; Hilgendorff2016]; no retrieved guideline uses the words first-line for oxygen, and iNO is named the first-line pulmonary vasodilator [CHOP2026].

evidence.quote: Oxygen is one of the most potent pulmonary vasodilators and increased oxygenation is the primary mediator of the reduction in PVR at birth.
evidence.location: Mechanism of pulmonary vasculature remodeling section

evidence.quote: Avoiding hypoxemia by mechanical ventilation and high concentrations of oxygen is the mainstay of PPHN management (5, 12).
evidence.location: Mechanism of pulmonary vasculature remodeling section

evidence.quote: Adequate oxygenation to achieve preductal PaO2 in the 50–80 mmHg range (similar to normal neonates) remains the cornerstone of PPHN management
the term or preterm newborn infant should receive oxygen, ventilatory support and/or surfactant if needed to achieve a preductal SpO 2 between 91% and 95% when PH is suspected or established
evidence.location: Table of recommendations (Class I, Level A)

evidence.quote: Inhaled nitric oxide is supported by high-quality evidence demonstrating improved oxygenation and reduced ECMO utilization, establishing it as first-line pulmonary vasodilator therapy in term and near-term neonates.

claims.manual_text: - If an infant has the following documented in the ECHO report, it is reasonable to keep FiO<sub>2</sub> at 0.4-0.6 (or higher if needed) with a post-ductal SpO<sub>2</sub> goal of ≥ 92-95% for 24-48 hrs until a repeat ECHO for reassessment is performed: - Estimated right ventricular (RV) pressure > 2/3 of systemic mean blood pressure (SBP<sup>mean</sup>) taken at the time of the ECHO study, (and/or) - Bidirectional PDA shunt.
claims.summary: Guidance sets the target at the pre-ductal site (91-95% EPPVDN, 92-97% Ball, 93-97% CHOP, 90-97% in an expert review, which suggests 93-98% in selected cases of acute severe PPHN, including FiO2 <0.6, and 95-98% in one UK network as reported in a review) and CHOP says post-ductal saturation should not independently guide decisions [Hilgendorff2016; Ball2023; CHOP2026; Lakshminrusimha2024; Mohamed2026]; RV pressure ≥2/3 systemic (systolic) and bidirectional ductal shunting appear only as trial entry criteria or severity markers [ElKhuffash2023; Titolo2025], and no retrieved source ties an FiO2 range or a 24-48 hour oxygen course to those findings.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests oxygen is titrated to pre-ductal SpO2, mostly within 90-97%, with values above 97% avoided in most guidance, although one review suggests 93-98% in selected severe cases, including when FiO2 is <0.6, and one UK network uses 95-98% [Hilgendorff2016; Ball2023; CHOP2026; Lakshminrusimha2024; Mohamed2026]; post-ductal saturation tracks shunting [Ball2023; CHOP2026]. No randomized trial defines the best target [Lakshminrusimha2024]. A review quotes an AHA/ATS caution that FiO2 >0.6 may be ineffective and may aggravate lung injury [Lakshminrusimha2024].

evidence.quote: Target pre-ductal oxygen saturation of 93–97% should guide oxygen titration and ventilator adjustments.
Post-ductal oxygen saturation should be monitored to assess differential shunting but should not independently guide therapeutic decisions.
Target pre-ductal saturations between 92 and 97%.
In our unit, we utilize post-ductal saturations to trend shunting indicating PH severity, but titrate supplemental oxygen based on pre-ductal saturation goals.

preductal SpO 2 between 91% and 95% when PH is suspected or established; lung hyperinflation and atelectasis, or lung collapse and intermittent desaturations below 85%, or hyperoxia with preductal SpO 2 above 97% should be avoided
evidence.location: Table of recommendations (Class I, Level A)

evidence.quote: There are no randomized clinical trials guiding optimal SpO2 targets in the management of PH in neonates.
Based on available evidence from animal studies and expert opinion, we recommend preductal SpO2 target of 90–97% in the management of acute PPHN in late preterm and term infants.

The American Heart Association (AHA) and American Thoracic Society (ATS) caution that extreme hyperoxia (FiO2 > 0.6) may be ineffective owing to extrapulmonary shunt in PPHN and aggravate lung injury.46
evidence.location: Upper limit of oxygen target range: Oxygen toxicity and lung

evidence.quote: A tricuspid regurgitant jet with a pressure gradient ≥ 2/3 systemic systolic blood pressure
Patent ductus arteriosus bidirectional shunting or predominant right to left shunting
bidirectional or right-to-left shunting suggests suprasystemic PH requiring aggressive vasodilation and inotropic support, while left-to-right shunting reflects milder disease.

Targeting slightly higher range at 93–98% may be prudent in the following situations with acute severe PPHN: (a) when FiO2 is <0.6 and risk of lung toxicity is low, (b) pH < 7.25, (c) therapeutic hypothermia, (d) lactic acidosis, and (e) probably in patients with dark skin pigmentation.
Pre-ductal SpO₂ 95-98%, aiming to narrow the pre- to post-ductal gap to below 5%
evidence.location: Table 2, section A (UK regional network guideline v2, 2024, reported second-hand)

claims.manual_text: *Note: PDA in an infant ≥ 35 weeks’ GA with severe PPHN may serve as a pop-off valve and therefore should not be managed the same way as a PDA in a very preterm infant with significant respiratory support requirement.*
claims.summary: A patent duct is described as a pop-off for a failing, pressure-loaded right ventricle, and guidance allows PGE1 to keep it open in selected infants [Singh2021; Siefkes2021; CHOP2026; Hilgendorff2016; Titolo2025]; no source sets a gestational-age limit or compares this with duct management in very preterm infants.

evidence.quote: Critically unwell infants with failing right ventricle may benefit from a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA), which can work as a “pop off” valve in cases with severely elated PVR.
evidence.location: Role of prostaglandin E1 in management of PPHN

evidence.quote: An open PDA might benefit the RV by providing a pop-off mechanism to reduce RV afterload.
Prostaglandin E₁ may be used to maintain ductal patency in select neonates with right ventricular dysfunction.

The preterm and term neonate with severe PH (PPHN) and no post-tricuspid-unrestrictive shunt (e.g, no VSD) may receive Prostaglandin E (PGE) 1 or PGE2 to maintain ductal patency in right heart failure
evidence.location: Table of recommendations (Class IIa, Level B)

evidence.quote: Prostaglandin E1 (PGE1) represents another valuable adjunct in infants with a constricting ductus arteriosus and RV failure, as maintaining ductal patency can create a “pop-off” mechanism that reduces RV afterload via right-to-left shunting.

claims.manual_text: - If oxygen therapy is the only intervention for PPHN, consider discontinuing when RV pressure is < 1/3 of SBP<sup>mean</sup>:
claims.summary: No retrieved source gives an RV-pressure threshold for stopping oxygen; CHOP lists optimal timing of repeat echocardiography as an evidence gap [CHOP2026], and the nearest advice is to avoid rapid weans [Ball2023].

evidence.quote: Evidence Gap: Minimum echocardiographic requirements in resource-limited settings, optimal timing for repeat echocardiography following initiation of pulmonary vasodilators, and routine necessity of pre-discharge echocardiography in all neonates.
Finally, avoid rapid weans, which may precipitate rapid decompensation.

claims.manual_text: - It will become evident that oxygen therapy is working in this respect when the pre-ductal and post-ductal SpO<sub>2</sub> show decreasing discrepancy and eventually equate to each other. This point signifies that shunting from right to left across the PDA has essentially been counterbalanced by pulmonary vasodilation.
claims.summary: The pre- to post-ductal split is used as a marker of PH severity and of response to therapy, and a narrowing gap as a bedside sign of improving pulmonary blood flow [Ball2023; Mohamed2026], but the gap can also be absent with low RV output, a small or closed duct, or atrial or balanced shunting [Mohamed2026; Lakshminrusimha2015].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests a narrowing gap tracks improving pulmonary blood flow [Ball2023; Mohamed2026]. Equal saturations do not by themselves show that right-to-left shunting has resolved, because the gap can also disappear with low RV output, a small or closed duct, or atrial or balanced shunting [Mohamed2026; Lakshminrusimha2015].

evidence.quote: Trending this degree of “split” between pre-ductal and post-ductal saturations is a helpful longitudinal marker of pulmonary hypertension (PH) severity and can demonstrate important minute-to-minute changes in pulmonary vasoconstriction in response to therapies or environment.
Conversely, a narrowing gap during treatment is a useful bedside sign of improving pulmonary blood flow [1].
evidence.location: Review: Figure 2 discussion (UK network guidance, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: The gap may be absent when right ventricular output is low, the ductus is small or closed, or shunting is predominantly atrial or balanced across both shunts [1,3].
evidence.location: Review: Figure 2 discussion (UK guidelines, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: If the PDA is closed and the shunt exclusively is at the PFO level, the degree of cyanosis is similar in both the upper and lower limbs.

claims.manual_text: - One of the major goals of any PPHN intervention is to equalize pre-ductal and post-ductal SpO<sub>2</sub> (within 2 points).
claims.summary: No source gives a target of within 2 points; one UK network, reported second-hand, aims for a gap below 5% [Mohamed2026], a one-centre guideline trends the gap as a severity marker [Ball2023], and CHOP says post-ductal saturation should not independently guide decisions [CHOP2026].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests the saturation gap is followed as a marker of shunting and response, and CHOP advises that post-ductal saturation not independently guide decisions [Ball2023; CHOP2026]. One UK network, reported in a review, sets a gap below 5% as a treatment aim, the only numeric aim found [Mohamed2026].

evidence.quote: Pre-ductal SpO₂ 95-98%, aiming to narrow the pre- to post-ductal gap to below 5%
evidence.location: Table 2, section A (UK regional network guideline v2, 2024, reported second-hand)

evidence.quote: Trending this degree of “split” between pre-ductal and post-ductal saturations is a helpful longitudinal marker of pulmonary hypertension (PH) severity
Post-ductal oxygen saturation should be monitored to assess differential shunting but should not independently guide therapeutic decisions.

claims.manual_text: - All infants ≥ 35 weeks’ GA needing FiO<sub>2</sub> > 0.8 for over 1 hr should be intubated and arterial access secured in anticipation of requiring iNO therapy and frequent blood tests while receiving iNO therapy.
claims.summary: Arterial access is recommended for ventilated or severe PPHN [CHOP2026; Ball2023], but no source was found for FiO2 >0.8 for over 1 hour as an intubation trigger; the only numeric figure is one UK network's 45-50% oxygen on non-invasive support, reported second-hand [Mohamed2026].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests arterial access for blood pressure monitoring and frequent sampling in PPHN [CHOP2026; Ball2023]. Intubation thresholds are sparsely defined: UK network guidance, reported in a review, advises a low threshold, with one network considering intubation above 45-50% oxygen on non-invasive support [Mohamed2026].

evidence.quote: Arterial access is recommended for continuous blood pressure monitoring and frequent blood sampling, with prioritization of the right upper extremity when feasible.
Umbilical Arterial Catheters (UAC) are indicated for all ventilated PPHN patients to permit monitoring of serial blood gases and blood pressure.

Network guidance advises a low threshold for intubation. One network recommends considering intubation in an infant requiring more than 45-50% oxygen to maintain saturations on non-invasive support [1].

claims.manual_text: *iNO therapy is not indicated in infants < 35 weeks’ GA per unit policy.*
claims.summary: The iNO boundary sits between 34 and 35 weeks: FDA labelling as cited in a review gives >34 weeks and the pooled pivotal trials enrolled ≥34 weeks [Singh2021; Golombek2010], while AAP refers to preterm infants as ≤34 weeks and CPS uses a <35-week heading, under which it does not recommend routine use but allows rescue use in selected cases [Kumar2014; Mitra2023]; Cochrane finds rescue iNO does not appear effective in very ill preterm infants [Barrington2017].
claims.note: Current evidence suggests rescue iNO may be considered below 35 weeks in selected cases: CPS names early-onset refractory HRF after PROM or oligohydramnios, and HRF or severe RV failure in BPD-PH [Mitra2023]. Cochrane finds rescue iNO does not appear effective in the very ill preterm infant [Barrington2017]. FDA labelling, as cited in a review, and the pivotal trials begin at about 34 weeks [Singh2021; Golombek2010].

evidence.quote: iNO is the only therapy approved by the US Food and Drug Administration for clinical use in term or near-term newborn infants (>34 weeks’ gestation) with hypoxemic respiratory failure with clinical or echocardiographic evidence of PPHN (5).
in term and late preterm (gestational age > or = 34 weeks) infants with HRF who required mechanical ventilation
Several randomized controlled trials have evaluated its role in the management of preterm infants ≤ 34 weeks' gestational age with varying results.

Routine iNO use in preterm infants on respiratory support is not recommended. iNO may be considered as a rescue modality in preterm infants with early-onset refractory HRF when associated with PROM or oligohydramnios.
evidence.location: Use in preterm infants born <35 weeks gestational age

evidence.quote: Recommendation: In preterm infants with HRF or severe RV failure in the context of BPD-PH, rescue therapy with iNO may be considered if other respiratory management strategies, such as optimized ventilator support or postnatal corticosteroids (or both), have failed to resolve the hypoxemic crisis or RV failure.
evidence.location: Use in preterm infants born <35 weeks gestational age

evidence.quote: iNO does not appear to be effective as rescue therapy for the very ill preterm infant.

claims.manual_text: - Infants with clinical suspicion of PPHN must have an ECHO done as soon as possible but should not wait for ECHO to initiate oxygen therapy.
claims.summary: CHOP gives a strong recommendation for echocardiography as soon as possible in suspected PPHN and allows for iNO started before echo [CHOP2026], and avoiding hypoxemia is described as the mainstay of care [Singh2021]; no recommendation addresses delaying oxygen for echo directly.

evidence.quote: Echocardiography should be obtained as soon as possible in neonates with suspected PPHN, particularly in neonates ≥ 34 weeks gestation with significant hypoxemia or a pre- to post-ductal saturation gradient.
If iNO is initiated prior to echocardiographic assessment and severe left ventricular dysfunction is subsequently identified, discontinuation of iNO is recommended.
Avoiding hypoxemia by mechanical ventilation and high concentrations of oxygen is the mainstay of PPHN management (5, 12).
evidence.location: Mechanism of pulmonary vasculature remodeling section

claims.manual_text: - Initial ECHO is also used to rule out congenital heart disease, shunting, and left ventricular (LV) function (see contraindications).
claims.summary: Guidance asks the first echo to exclude congenital heart disease, define shunts and assess left ventricular function before pulmonary vasodilators [CHOP2026; Ball2023; Mitra2023].

evidence.quote: Echocardiographic assessment should include evaluation of right and left ventricular systolic function, shunt direction and magnitude, and estimation of pulmonary artery pressure.
Finally, cyanotic CCHD is a major disease process in the differential diagnosis of PPHN, so complete echocardiograms should be obtained to fully evaluate the cardiac and vascular anatomy.
Echocardiographic confirmation of normal left ventricular function and absence of congenital heart disease characterized by ductal-dependent systemic blood flow before initiating iNO are recommended.
evidence.location: Recommendation, Use in late-preterm and term infants

claims.manual_text: - Infants with ECHO-confirmed PPHN should have serial ECHOs every 24-72 hours until complete resolution of PPHN.
claims.summary: Repeat echocardiography is supported, especially in moderate to severe PPHN with hemodynamic instability [Singh2021], but CHOP ties it to clinical change or therapy changes and lists optimal timing as an evidence gap [CHOP2026], and no retrieved source gives a 24-72 hour interval.
claims.note: Current evidence suggests serial echocardiography timed by clinical change, changes in therapy, poor vasodilator response or planned iNO weaning rather than by a fixed interval [Singh2021; CHOP2026]. CHOP lists optimal repeat timing as an evidence gap and recommends a pre-discharge study to confirm resolution [CHOP2026].

evidence.quote: We recommend serial echocardiography (Figure 5) assessment to monitor the disease progress, changing pathophysiology and response to treatment in PPHN, especially in infants with moderate to severe PPHN with hemodynamic instability (Figure 6).
Repeat echocardiography should be guided by clinical change, escalation or de-escalation of therapy, lack of response to pulmonary vasodilators, or planned weaning of inhaled nitric oxide.
evidence.location: Timing and Frequency of Echocardiography (Conditional Recommendation)

evidence.quote: A pre-discharge echocardiogram, ideally obtained off respiratory support, is recommended by pediatric cardiology to confirm resolution of pulmonary hypertension and guide outpatient follow-up.
evidence.location: Timing and Frequency of Echocardiography (Strong Recommendation)

evidence.quote: Evidence Gap: Minimum echocardiographic requirements in resource-limited settings, optimal timing for repeat echocardiography following initiation of pulmonary vasodilators, and routine necessity of pre-discharge echocardiography in all neonates.

claims.manual_text: - Correct pH to > 7.30. Maintaining pH as close to physiological range as possible is crucial for achieving hemodynamic stability. Forced alkalosis does not lead to further improvement.
claims.summary: CHOP and a one-centre guideline set pH at 7.30-7.40 or ≥7.3 in critically ill infants, others accept >7.25 with 7.30-7.40 preferred, and UK guidance cites 7.35-7.45 [CHOP2026; Ball2023; Lakshminrusimha2015; Hilgendorff2016; Mohamed2026]; induced alkalosis is discouraged, Ball noting it lowers PVR but reduces tissue oxygen delivery [Ball2023; Lakshminrusimha2015; Mohamed2026], although body text in the EPPVDN paper names pH 7.45-7.55, against its own table [Hilgendorff2016].

evidence.quote: Arterial pH should be maintained within the target range of 7.30–7.40 to support myocardial performance and limit pulmonary vasoconstriction.
evidence.location: Acid-Base Management and Sodium Bicarbonate (Strong Recommendation)

evidence.quote: Goal arterial pH ≥ 7.3 while critically ill. A more permissive pH >7.25 target may be acceptable once clinical stability has been achieved.
While alkalosis effectively decreases PVR, it decreases tissue oxygen delivery, impairs cerebral perfusion and is associated with hearing loss and poorer neurodevelopmental outcomes.1,37
We recommend maintaining pH greater than 7.25, preferably 7.30 to 7.40, during the acute phase of PPHN.
Hyperventilation and infusion of alkali were used in the past but should be avoided because of adverse effects on cerebral perfusion and increased risk of sensorineural deafness.
a pCO 2 between 45 and 60 mm Hg and a target pH >7.25 with lactate <5 mmol/L can be considered as target values.
evidence.location: Table of recommendations (Class IIa, Level B)

evidence.quote: Optimisation of the acid-base balance ( pH range 7.45 –7.55) to control PVR may require repetitive doses of sodium bicarbonate
PaCO₂ 4.5-5.5 kPa with pH 7.35-7.45

known_limitations: Several hemodynamic sources are single-institution or pathway documents (CHOP2026, Ball2023, Iowa Neonatology Handbook) and UK network values are reported second-hand in Mohamed2026; AHA/ATS content appears only as quoted in reviews.

ELSO OI thresholds come from the ELSO neonatal supplement v1.3 (2013); Mohamed2026's 'v1.4 (2017)' label for the same URL could not be confirmed. Wild2020 (ELSO 2020) Figure 1 is an image, transcribed by hand.
Iowa Inotropes and Vasopressor Table quotes are read from a PDF table's text extraction, checked against a rendered image.
Omission o1 (infection caution with hydrocortisone) passes the omission test narrowly and rests on a one-centre guideline and a review.
The saved Abman2015 page was a bot check, logged and not worked around; Abman2015 and Hansmann2019 were read as abstracts only.
Kumar2014's citation leaves out the corporate author (Committee on Fetus and Newborn, AAP); refs.py does not carry PubMed collective names.
